items.title: Identifying Angles that Map a Polygon Onto Itself

sections.normalized_html:
The square shown above is rotated about its center [MATH: O.] Which of the following angles of rotation would carry the rotated square onto itself?

  1. [MATH: 180^\circ]

  2. [MATH: 160^\circ]

  3. [MATH: 270^\circ]

[IMG: /graphics/e20d3aa412b863e775b0fb36b9b489a8]

The square shown above is rotated about its center [MATH: O.] Which of the following angles of rotation would carry the rotated square onto itself?

1. [MATH: 180^\circ]
2. [MATH: 160^\circ]
3. [MATH: 270^\circ]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If we rotate a square about its center by multiples of [MATH: \dfrac{360^\circ}{4} = 90^\circ,] we get the same square.

Among the given options, the multiples of [MATH: 90^\circ] are

  • [MATH: 2 \cdot 90^\circ = 180^\circ,] and

  • [MATH: 3 \cdot 90^\circ = 270^\circ.]

Therefore, a rotation by an angle of [MATH: 180^\circ] or [MATH: 270^\circ] will carry the rotated square onto itself.

So, the correct answer is "I and III only."

Content:
The order of rotational symmetry of a figure is the number of times the figure lies perfectly on top of itself as we rotate it through an angle of [MATH: 360^\circ.]

Content:
To demonstrate, let's consider an equilateral triangle. What is its order of rotational symmetry?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/057284048cfaab3309c156de4067fef9]

Content:
An equilateral triangle is a regular polygon with [MATH: {\color{blue}3}] sides.

Content:
To compute the smallest angle that we can rotate the figure so that it appears unchanged, we divide [MATH: 360^\circ] by [MATH: {\color{blue}{3}},] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{360^\circ}{\color{blue}3} = 120^\circ]

Content:
So, we can rotate the triangle about its center by [MATH: 120^\circ] a total of [MATH: \color{blue}3] times before the triangle's vertices return to their original position.

Content:
Therefore, the order of rotational symmetry of an equilateral triangle is [MATH: {\color{blue}{3}}.]

Content:
In general, the order of rotational symmetry of a regular [MATH: n]-gon is [MATH: n.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Order of Rotational Symmetry

Content:
The order of rotational symmetry of a figure is the number of times the figure lies perfectly on top of itself as we rotate it through an angle of [MATH: 360^\circ.]

Content:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/057284048cfaab3309c156de4067fef9]

Content:
An equilateral triangle is a regular polygon with [MATH: {\color{blue}3}] sides.

Content:
To compute the smallest angle that we can rotate the figure so that it appears unchanged, we divide [MATH: 360^\circ] by [MATH: {\color{blue}{3}},] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{360^\circ}{\color{blue}3} = 120^\circ]

Content:
So, we can rotate the triangle about its center by [MATH: 120^\circ] a total of [MATH: \color{blue}3] times before the triangle's vertices return to their original position.

Content:
Therefore, the order of rotational symmetry of an equilateral triangle is [MATH: {\color{blue}{3}}.]

Content:
In general, the order of rotational symmetry of a regular [MATH: n]-gon is [MATH: n.]
